questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain the following terms as used in reproduction.

(i) Pathernogenesis.

(ii) Capacitation.

(iii) Cortical reaction.

(iv) Ovulation. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Parthenogenesis** (printed "Pathernogenesis"). A type of **asexual reproduction in which an unfertilised egg develops into a new individual** without the fusion of gametes. The egg may be haploid (e.g. the male bee, the **drone**, is a haploid parthenogenetic male) or diploid (e.g. **aphids** and *Daphnia* in summer, where diploid eggs develop by mitosis). It gives rapid population growth when conditions are good. It can also be induced artificially in frog and sea urchin eggs by pricking or by chemicals.

**(ii) Capacitation.** The **final maturation of sperm in the female reproductive tract** (in the uterus and oviduct, taking about 7 hours in humans) before they are able to fertilise an egg. Secretions of the female tract **remove the coating of seminal-plasma proteins and cholesterol** from the sperm head membrane, so that the membrane over the acrosome becomes **fragile and permeable to calcium ions**; the sperm becomes **hyperactive** (more vigorous tail movement) and can undergo the **acrosome reaction** on meeting the egg.

**(iii) Cortical reaction.** The reaction of the egg **just after the entry of the sperm head**. **Cortical granules** (lysosome-like vesicles lying under the egg membrane) **fuse with the plasma membrane and release enzymes** into the space between the membrane and the zona pellucida (perivitelline space). These enzymes **harden the zona pellucida** (the fertilisation membrane) and destroy the sperm-binding receptors, so that **no more sperm can enter (block to polyspermy)**.

**(iv) Ovulation.** The **release of a secondary oocyte (arrested at metaphase of meiosis II) from a mature Graafian follicle** through the wall of the ovary into the funnel of the oviduct, at about **day 14 of the menstrual cycle** in women. It is triggered by a sudden surge of **luteinising hormone (LH)** from the anterior pituitary, itself caused by a high oestrogen concentration.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the process of spermatogenesis in Humans. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Spermatogenesis** is the formation of spermatozoa (sperm). It takes place in the **seminiferous tubules of the testes** and starts at puberty; the whole process takes about 64 to 74 days. The germinal epithelium of the tubule shows the stages from the outside (basement membrane) to the lumen:

1. **Multiplication phase.** The **spermatogonia** (diploid, $2n = 46$) in the outer layer of the tubule divide repeatedly by **mitosis**. Some remain as stem cells; others grow.
2. **Growth phase.** Some spermatogonia enlarge, take in food from the **Sertoli (nurse) cells** and become **primary spermatocytes** (still diploid, $2n$).
3. **Maturation phase (meiosis).** Each primary spermatocyte undergoes **meiosis I**, giving **two secondary spermatocytes** (haploid, $n = 23$); each secondary spermatocyte undergoes **meiosis II**, so that one primary spermatocyte gives **four haploid spermatids**.
4. **Differentiation (spermiogenesis).** Each spermatid, attached to a Sertoli cell, changes into a **spermatozoon** without dividing: the **Golgi body forms the acrosome** (cap with digestive enzymes) over the nucleus, the **nucleus condenses** to form the head, one **centriole** forms the axial filament of the **flagellum (tail)**, **mitochondria** gather as a spiral sheath in the **middle piece**, and most of the **cytoplasm is lost**.
5. The mature sperm are released into the lumen of the tubule and carried to the **epididymis**, where they become motile and are stored until ejaculation.

**Summary:** spermatogonium ($2n$) $\to$ (mitosis) primary spermatocyte ($2n$) $\to$ (meiosis I) 2 secondary spermatocytes ($n$) $\to$ (meiosis II) 4 spermatids ($n$) $\to$ (differentiation) 4 spermatozoa ($n$).

**Drawing expected (rewarded):** a transverse section of a seminiferous tubule with spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, Sertoli cell, sperm in the lumen and the interstitial (Leydig) cells between tubules, all labelled.

questions.enonce_markdown: How is spermatogenesis hormonally controlled in Humans? *[5 marks]* *(8, 7, 5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Spermatogenesis is controlled by hormones of the **hypothalamus, the anterior pituitary and the testes**, with **negative feedback**.

1. At puberty the **hypothalamus** secretes **gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH)**, which stimulates the **anterior pituitary** to secrete **FSH** (follicle stimulating hormone) and **LH** (luteinising hormone, also called ICSH, interstitial cell stimulating hormone).
2. **LH** acts on the **interstitial (Leydig) cells** between the seminiferous tubules to secrete **testosterone**.
3. **FSH** acts on the **Sertoli cells** of the tubules, which nourish the developing sperm and secrete **androgen-binding protein**, so that a high concentration of testosterone is kept inside the tubule. **Testosterone and FSH together stimulate** the development of the spermatogonia into sperm (spermatogenesis); testosterone also maintains the accessory glands and the **secondary sexual characters**.
4. **Negative feedback:** a high concentration of **testosterone** inhibits the secretion of GnRH by the hypothalamus and of LH by the pituitary; the Sertoli cells secrete **inhibin**, which inhibits the secretion of FSH by the anterior pituitary. When the sperm count and testosterone fall, the inhibition is lifted and secretion rises again, so sperm production remains fairly constant.
